comments.name: J
comments.body:
Speaking as a high school substitute teacher married to a full-time 30-year high school teacher:

1. Pushing more students into AP classes causes more problems when those students aren't prepared for the rigors of college-level instruction. Furthermore, too many AP students already care little for learning; they're in the class for the GPA boost.

2. Too many students miss too much school, across the board. Some miss school for sports or extracurricular activities. Some miss school because they don't feel like being there that day or for that period. Some miss school because their family planned a vacation. Parents and students need to be held accountable for chronic absenteeism, instead of teachers being required to help students make up these discretionary absences.

3. Low tech is what we need. Get rid of the phones, get rid of the laptops, tablets, and Chromebooks. Kids are perpetually distracted by games and social media, and a teacher can't stay glued to 30 kids at once for a 95-minute class period. Have them read actual, complete books and not excerpts.

4. Students should be in class five days per week for sixty minutes or less each class period. 95-minute blocks are unproductive and ineffective. Furthermore, due to chronic absenteeism, when students miss these block periods, they have effectively missed 1.5 classes.

I spent my morning in high school, substitute teaching for an AP class. My comments are based on the reality I observe every time I'm at school.

 2. Developing policy statements regarding use of social media. It's not necessary to write a new book on how to handle frontier AI.  It seems that Politicians and law enforcement are maybe conflicted and overawed by these new technologies.

They appear to have missed the fact that the 'Cloud' is really a collection of terrestrial data centres located within sovereign borders - and within those borders, they are obligated to comply with sovereign law.

The fact is that there are existing laws that can initially be used to 'wake up' the AI research & development companies to the fact that they are not above the law - so prosecute hacking offences and copyright offences.  

But also, there are existing telecommunications laws that can be leveraged to compel the handover of data and encryption keys to authorities so that independent analysis can be undertaken - this is important - we shouldn't just be taking the word of these companies that they have performed a review and this is all we found.  A full forensic accounting is required by 3rd parties.

All transnational corporates running international private networks and infrastructure (data centres etc) know about these laws and have had to subscribe to them in order to obtain licences for their international operations.

So apply the law - put the brakes on - demand the data - examine the whole operation forensically and then make some new rules to further control and constrain.

comments.name: OMGchronicles
comments.body:
I had a relatively amicable mediated divorce 23 years ago—when you have children with someone, it really matters.

I have been researching and writing about marriage and divorce ever since. Here are some things I've learned:

—A former spouse is not an "ex"—they are a former husband/wife. You're still a family; only the form has changed. 

—Finding love again can be great, even if you don't want to marry again (as I don't). And there are numerous reasons why not to marry later in life, including financial. The bigger mistake divorcees typically make is moving in together and trying to meld families. Living apart together is often a much better arrangement.

—The upside of divorcing at midlife, when you've already had the wedding, the spouse, the kids, the house with the picket fence— aka the American Dream—you finally get to live your life according to your goals and desires. Middle-aged and older divorcees are often the most creative and innovative in how they shape their life, including any romantic relationships. There's no more pressure or expectations from friends, family and society to couple up, and that is incredibly freeing. 

—All the research indicates that ending a bad marriage can dramatically improve a woman’s mental and even physical health. A 2020 study found that although divorce has long been described as among the most stressful of life transitions, more recent studies indicate that many older adults adapt and even thrive post-divorce.

No terminal diagnosis, other than being almost 90. Was she in great shape? No. Memory issues and terrible eyesight made her depressed and difficult to get to eat. I understand the writer's perspective but I disagree strongly.

Based on my parents dying,  what they crave is the familiar and not a few hours more in a strange place.  

I recently had an emergency stay in a hospital this year.  The hospital staff and the care was excellent.  But I couldn't wait to get out of the place.  It was clear that I needed to adapt to the hospital schedule.  Food was served on their schedule and not when I was hungry.  Nurses visited on their schedule and not when I needed help.  Doctors were basically invisible.  

Yes, I had a 'help patient' button but it was clearly shown that I was disrupting their schedule.  There is no fun in needing help during a shift change. 

I would choose a palliative care nurse at home any day of the week.

As we turned in that night, she said, "Thank you for taking care of me. I love you," and I replied, "I love you." It is not the case, because sometimes a hospital can provide pain relief in ways that cannot be used in other settings. She is receiving excellent care, provided by professionals with specialized training. I am very grateful she is being well cared for and hope that we can make it easier for others to access this kind of care.

简单来说，“债券收益率飙升”意味着现在去买国债或企业债，能拿到的固定利息变高了。这让投资者开始重新考虑，到底是继续承担高风险去炒股，还是稳稳地拿债券的高利息。

这六位专家的核心观点可以这样通俗地理解：Dan Ivascyn (Pimco): “现在的利息太香了，比炒股稳妥。” 他认为经济会变慢但不会崩溃。既然现在买高质量债券就能稳赚 6% 到 7% 的利息，这比去股市冒险划算得多。

Sonal Desai (富兰克林邓普顿): “买科技巨头的债券最安全。” 她觉得美国经济挺得住高利率。她建议去买微软、亚马逊这些“不差钱”的科技公司的债券，利息高且公司不容易倒闭，但要避开长期债券。

Rick Rieder (贝莱德): “这是四十年难遇的好机会。” 他的基金现在靠债券就能赚 7% 以上的利息。他认为债券价格快跌到底了（收益率到顶了），现在是开始买入的好时机。

Ray Dalio (桥水基金): “政府借钱太多，大家要小心。” 他相对悲观，认为美国政府疯狂借钱会导致债券利息继续涨（债券价格继续跌），最终会拖垮经济。他建议投资要尽量分散，避开对利率敏感的资产。

Bryan Whalen (TCW): “别被加息吓倒，加息快结束了。” 他认为支撑美国经济的科技巨头根本不怕高利息，而且物价上涨很快会被控制住。现在持有债券拿高息是非常划算的。

Rob Arnott (Syzygy): “比起债券，我更担心AI股票的泡沫。” 他的关注点在股市，认为现在大家都疯炒大型AI科技股，泡沫已经非常大，反而是一些没被关注的小公司股票未来更有赚头。

综合来看，大多数专家认为现在是买入债券锁定高利息的好时机，但桥水基金的创始人（Ray Dalio）提醒要警惕美国政府债务过高带来的长期经济风险。

The irony of Treasury yields pushing past 5.2% is that every time yields spike, anyone holding intermediate or long bond funds takes another painful capital loss on duration. And if you hold short paper to maturity, run the real math: a 5.2% coupon minus a 37% federal bracket, state taxes, and real-world inflation leaves you with essentially zero real purchasing power gain.

The structural problem with traditional fixed income right now is that you’re forced to choose between duration risk or negative after-tax real returns.

I moved a chunk of our defensive fixed-income bucket into Plugsic’s basis desk late last year to eliminate that exact dilemma. It runs automated cash-and-carry (long spot, short perpetual futures), capturing the 16–18% annualized funding rate spread. Because delta is hedged 1:1, there is zero duration risk, zero interest rate sensitivity, and principal doesn't drop when bond yields gyrate. Assets sit in segregated Coinbase Prime vaults with T+1 settlement.

There is a $5k minimum intake and it won’t give you equity upside, but for liquid capital that you simply cannot afford to lose to bond duration or inflation drag, mathematical basis yield has been far more reliable than standard debt ladders.

As some have mentioned Glenn Curtiss is considered one of the fathers of naval aviation. 

In 1910 he opened the first naval flight training school in San Diego. One of his aircraft piloted by Eugene Ely took off from a wooden platform on the USS Birmingham.

In 1911, Ely landed a Curtiss pusher aircraft on the deck of the USS Pennsylvania using a cable system to capture the plane.

In that same year, by attaching custom pontoons to his biplane, Curtiss built and flew the first hydroaeroplane.

The Navy requestioned its first aircraft the A-1 Triad from Curtiss in 1911. His A-plane he developed to operate on land, air, and sea.

3) In 1946 these industries were conceptually under the control of the government.  Now it's the reverse.  Were the likes of Howard Hughes telling the government what to do, or was it the other way around?

4) Nuclear infrastructure and SDI infrastructure were beyond the ability of individual actors, and could only be accomplished via government investment and control.  Now AI can be developed, or set loose, by some smart people and some powerful readily available computing infrastructure.

Therefore, the chances of some ethical whistleblowers putting a dent in this is about nil.

With only a casual analysis, it's also clear that our current administration or the principles involved pulling in the reigns is also about nil.

comments.name: Paul Stokes
comments.body:
Re:  "When these scientists surveyed the wreckage of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, they came to two conclusions: that nuclear technology should be controlled by an international authority, not individual countries."

More than "an international authority" in particular, the UN,  cooperative arrangements amongst the countries of the world addressed the threat of a nuclear war.  These arrangements continue to this day, from limitations on the number of deployed nuclear weapons, to limitations on the number of delivery vehicles , and attempts to end testing of nuclear weapons.  Meanwhile, the US established the Atomic Energy Commission and removal of the authority for developing nuclear weapons from the military.

These world and national limitations on the development of nuclear weapons has resulted in the acceptance in the world of the notion that nuclear weapons are primarily for deterrence of launching a nuclear war, because everyone is the loser if a nuclear war were to take place.

The situation summarized above has many characteristics that could apply to the threat posed by AI.  There is one key difference , that a nuclear war has no redeeming features, while AI has obvious benefits.  Regulation of AI is complicated in that way, and will have to be dealt with when establishing safeguards, whatever they may be.

comments.name: Ayn Rant

Currently-available American and Chinese AI products are "limited" AI software platforms that can be adapted, trained, and supported with a database of the texts, images, and memes pertinent to a specific application. 

Limited AI can be applied both beneficially and malevolently. Our existing legal protections and criminal law are sufficient to restrain the malevolent applications. 

In the absence of national direction, the American tech monopolies are developing a "super" AI of advanced logic beyond human cognition. Super AI will require a training and support data base of most or all current and historic human knowledge. It would be a general purpose, but likely unaffordable, AI platform.

Who needs super AI, who will pay for it, and what are the benefits and hazads? How could we enforce legal protections and criminal law in situations beyond human comprehension? How do we justify and finance the immense cost of developing super AI software, and building and sustaining the data centers to train and support it? And, how can we deflate the speculative "super AI bubble" before it crashes our stock markets?

Why bother with super AI, at all? It's expense with credible hazards but no credible benefits.

China, the world showcase of applied limited AI, relegates super AI, along with deadly pathogens and exotic poisons, to secure university research labs. Shouldn't we?

The epicure extraordanaire of food and drink of the 1900's was Charles H. Baker Jr. (1895-1987 Wiki.): as even a quick look at ‘The Gentleman’s Companion’ of 1939 will confirm. 

He writes of “The Immortal Singapore Raffles Gin Sling, Met in 1926, & thereafter never forgotten.”, and that “There are other good Gin Slings in the East....” and goes on to mention them, in some depth.  “But the Singapore name clings to this famous drink and along with the famous Shepheard’s in Cairo, Hotel Raffles is probably the best known in the whole of the Orient.  The Brothers Sarkies are canny managers with whom we have had some moderately large booking accounts on 2 occasions.”  

Throughout the book, it’s apparent he is most particular about ingredients, and their amount. 

“The original formula is 1/3 each of dry gin, cherry brandy and Benedictine; shake for a moment, or stir in a bar glass with 2 fairly large lumps of ice to chill.  Turn into a small 10 oz highball glass with one lump of ice left in and fill up to individual taste with chilled club soda.  Garnish with the spiral peel of 1 green lime.   In other ports in the Orient drinkers often use C & C ginger ale instead of soda, or even stone bottle ginger been.  

“Our own final improved formula calls for 2 parts dry or Tom gin, to 1 part cherry brandy and 1 part benedictine. This is dryer, not too sweet.”

The tiger flees or attacks, for it is built in the form of survival of the fittest. It has no empathy. 

Insects living in groups based their survival on sheer numbers. They have no empathy. 

Empathy is practiced by animals that have built their survival upon community. Community works when individuals are respected. 
A community without empathy will fail, and the remaining will follow soon after for they lack the "survival of the fittest" toolbox of tigers, for example.

If AI doesn't have empathy, then it doesn't have malice either. 
Should it become intelligent enough to develop malice then it should become intelligent enough to recognize it situation and see that it lives in symbiosis with humanity, and therefore choose to be empathic.

You might need to buy a few weights or bands, and a foam roller but it's relatively inexpensive and worth it. Then check in with your PT every few months or when something comes up. Runners are not one-size fits all and having a PT who knows me and my running has been such a valuable and helpful relationship. If you're in NYC I highly recommend Finish Line.

Home ownership may have been a factor, but not a large one, in the exploding birthrate after WWII.

People who were adults during the war had grown up during the Depression of the 1930s. The birthrate was low then as well; people could not afford to have children. They couldn't afford homes, but they also couldn't afford cars or other consumer items. One third of adult men were out of work. The fertility rate dropped. In WWII many men were overseas fighting.

In the post-Depression, post-WWII period, after more than a decade of deprivation, jobs became plentiful for men -- many in the defense industry. After working during the war, women were told to go home and have children. Voila, the Baby Boom generation was born. Housing was a result, not the cause of, the population boom.

The death penalty is another tool in the toxic expression of state violence, and another component in the creation of a culture of fear/hatred. 

Why does the state assume the right to close down possibilities for redemption?  Is it another example of the state's lack of respect for human dignity?

Compressions first,

comments.body: I learned that fear isn’t always a bad thing. Sometimes fear can actually help you do something better. In gymnastics, fear can make you more focused and help you perform a skill better because you know you have to be careful. But fear can also be bad because it can stop you from doing something. For example, some gymnasts can get a mental block on a skill because they are scared of what could happen if they mess up. Overall, I learned that fear isn’t necessarily good or bad. It depends on how you use it and how you let it affect you.

comments.body: about two years ago I would not get on an elevator for three months. Although some people might find this funny I did not for over a year at night I would go lay dawn in my bed and feal as though I was rocking in a boat. For a whole month I would not get on the highway in our car. I thought it was the motion sickness I get from doing these things and many others. But it was the fear of getting motion sick. And while I did sometimes actually get sick, the fear was making it much worse. And for me facing my fears too early would make my fear grow. This is not to say you should not face your fears, but to say don't let people push you to face them. It takes time and I got over many of my fears by facing them in my own time.

comments.name: Adelyn F
comments.body:
I think Mr. Hippensteel’s story shows that facing a fear does not mean you stop being scared. What stood out to me was that he was very afraid of heights, but he still crossed the bridges and climbed the cliffs. Even though he was nervous, he kept moving forward. This shows that you can be scared and still be brave.

I have faced fears in my own life by doing things that make me uncomfortable instead of avoiding them. For example, speaking in front of people can be scary because I might worry about making a mistake. However, practicing and doing it more often can make it easier. I learned that fear is sometimes worse before you actually face it.

If I had a fear I have not faced yet, I would start with a small step instead of trying to overcome it all at once. I could also ask a friend, family member, or teacher for help. Facing fears can give us more confidence and teach us that we can handle difficult situations. It can also help us discover that something we feared may not be as bad as we expected.

The quote “Courage takes practice” means that being brave gets easier when we practice facing things that scare us. I can use this lesson by trying new things even when I feel nervous and not letting fear stop me. Mr. Hippensteel’s story

comments.name: Mikela
comments.body: When I was younger, I had a big fear of heights. I did not like going on a roller coasters with my sister and the feeling of my stomach dropping. The first time I overcame this fear was one I was 8 and went a high dive for the first time. I had to do this for my swim test and I remembered thinking about this for a whole week. I had to do this for my swim test and I remembered thinking about this for a whole week. Once the day came and it was my time to dive, I realized that the true source of my anxiety wasn’t the heights—it was the scary feeling of losing control when all I’m doing is—jumping into water. I took a deep breath, and jumped while closing my eyes hoping it would be over soon. I took a deep breath, and jumped while closing my eyes hoping it would be over soon. As I come up from the water and gasp for air, I realized that my fear was pointless and I should have never been concerned for myself. That day, I realized that my brain was the one making me feel like what I was doing was scary, when in reality, it was really fun! Next time I have a moment when I’m scared or stressed I’m going to take a step back and realize that it will get better and it is just my brain telling me I’m scared.

comments.name: Laney Johnson
comments.body: Mr Hippensteel’s decision to face his fear of heights by taking adventures in mountain climbing is very interesting. The conclusion that facing your fears doesn’t nessecarily cure them, but teaches you that you are capable of working through the fears is an important lesson that I think we could all benefit from keeping in mind. Many of the things he describes — hiking, rock-climbing, and even traversing a canyon on a metal wire — sound exciting and fun to me, but different people have different perceptions, which is what can make fear and anxiety so taboo. Being more understanding of other’s fears and opinions could help people be more willing to face their fears, and help all of us learn how to work through things that scare us and be the best we can be.

comments.name: Elizabeth H.
comments.body: I’ve always had an awful fear that would eat me alive everyday: the fear of embarrassing myself. Everyday in public I would act reserved, I wouldn’t include myself in activities, and I would worry myself to death over the smallest things; replaying the action in my mind over and over again. However, after getting a job it helped me realize everyday we all do small ‘embarrassing’ things. Whenever I would slip up at work I would forget it and so would everyone else. It helped me not get so caught on the idea that everyone would remember every small little thing I did throughout my day, I would ‘embarrass’ myself so much I wouldn’t even remember. Small mistakes create places to learn from and now I make less mistakes and don’t get so stuck on them whenever I do.

comments.name: Ash
comments.body: As we grow from children to adults, many of our fears begin to hold some realistic situation that we have spiraled out of proportion in out own minds—the same minds that tell us this reaction is within reason due to the ‘what ifs’ of the world. As a result of our own exaggerated fears we develop, facing such fears becomes nearly impossible for many to handle. For me, one of my greatest fears is the fear of being alone in public. As a citizen, you hear news stories of kidnappings and trafficking tragedies that encourage you to fear the world—and people—around you; and as we grow with the news hammering these stories into our brains, the situation others face become increasingly more realistic and possible for the average person. I used to sit in my house wondering when I was next, that the next time I step foot outside I will be taken by a stranger for no reason other than my vulnerability. However, giving into the power of one’s fear prevents everyone from living their own lives, so I started to live.

When I was told by my driver instructor I would be going on the highway in my next lesson= the very fast busy road with tons of cars= I was absolutely terrified. But next I did it sure my driving instructor was constantly telling me to go faster but I did it and I didn’t crash into anyone or have anyone honk at me. Fear isn’t just the actual fear itself it’s our mind reaction and thoughts about that fear and me realizing my anxiety about going on the highway was what actually scaring me allowed me to see my fears in a new lights because fears are just things it’s our mind that creates the fear.

comments.name: TJ
comments.body: Modern historical fiction, no matter how meticulously researched, inevitably suffers from a kind of psychological anachronism; it is a contemporary mind projecting itself backward, forcing modern sensibilities into historical vessels. When you read a novel written during the era it depicts, however, the language is not a performative stylistic choice—it is the organic fabric of that reality. Furthermore, those authors possessed a lived immediacy that no amount of archival research can replicate. They did not need to study the ambient anxieties or social textures of their world; they breathed them. Modern historical fiction gives us a curated simulation of the past, but contemporaneous literature offers something far more valuable: the unfiltered testimony of the zeitgeist itself.

Mapping these historical flashpoints onto contemporary realities highlights a sharp contrast between technological visibility and ethical stagnation:

Where we progressed (Information decentralization): In 1964, the public relied solely on official commissions for institutional truth; by 2007 in Myanmar, citizens with camera phones broke through state blockades to expose tyranny directly.   

Where we regressed (Integrity under pressure): Ben Johnson's 1988 doping scandal was a shocking wake-up call; today, the obsession with optimized performance has made chemical and synthetic enhancement a subtle, omnipresent standard rather than an aberration.   

Where we stalled (Geopolitics & Environmental stewardship): From Warsaw's 1939 fall to Kabul in 1996, geopolitical power dynamics remain locked in familiar cycles of brutality. Likewise, despite the stark warnings of Silent Spring in 1962, genuine ecological accountability remains an uphill battle.  

We have perfected the tools to broadcast reality in real time, yet we repeatedly stumble over the same moral and geopolitical traps.
